title: CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 57 & 2022 FCA 178)
subject: TCC decision on whether repayable federal SADI contributions constituted government assistance reducing SR&ED ITCs.
keyPhrase: CAE Inc v The Queen 2021 TCC 57
summary: For Canadian corporations claiming SR&ED incentives, CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57, confirms that unconditionally repayable government loans on non-commercial terms are "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, reducing SR&ED expenditure pools and investment tax credits; the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed, rejecting any bifurcation of principal and interest subsidy.
metaDescription: Review the CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 57, affirmed 2022 FCA 178) SR&ED tax credit rulings in the Tax Court of Canada and FCA.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The litigation in CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57 (originally issued in French as CAE Inc. c. La Reine, 2021 CCI 57), affirmed unanimously from the bench by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (2022 CAF 178), and rendered final through the Supreme Court of Canada's dismissal of leave to appeal on May 25, 2023 (Docket 40504), stands as a watershed judicial authority in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax law. Adjudicated under the federal jurisdiction of Canada pursuant to the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the ITA), the dispute addressed a fundamental question of corporate tax law: whether unconditionally repayable, full-recourse loans or financial contributions disbursed by the federal Crown on non-commercial terms constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA in their entire principal amount, or merely to the extent of the concessional interest-rate subsidy embedded within the financing.
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

CAE Inc. (CAE), a Canadian public corporation founded in 1947 and headquartered in Ville Saint-Laurent, Quebec, primarily engaged in the manufacture, sale and maintenance of flight simulators and in flight-simulator training for the civil and military aviation industries, undertook a five-year SR&ED initiative designated as "Project Falcon", which required SR&ED expenditures of $700,000,000 from 2009 to 2014 and bore on the development of flight simulator and health sector technologies. To finance a portion of the substantial research costs associated with Project Falcon, CAE entered into a formal contribution agreement on March 30, 2009, with the Minister of Industry (Department of Industry Canada, subsequently Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada) under the federal Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) program. Designated as "SADI Agreement NO. 780-503924 - Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative - Project Falcon" (the SADI Agreement), the contract stipulated that Industry Canada would reimburse a specified percentage of CAE's eligible SR&ED costs incurred on Project Falcon, up to an aggregate funding ceiling of $250,000,000 over five years.

In its corporate income tax returns for the 2012 and 2013 taxation years, CAE treated the SADI disbursements received during those periods as ordinary commercial debt financing—specifically, full-recourse, non-forgivable capital loans. Because the SADI Agreement mandated unconditional repayment of the advances, CAE did not classify the principal receipts as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Consequently, CAE neither deducted the SADI inflows from its pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) nor reduced its "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(18) when calculating its SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITCs). Furthermore, CAE excluded the principal advances from its taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(x).
The Tax Authority's Challenge

In respect of CAE's 2012 and 2013 taxation years, the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), issued two assessments, dated October 26 and December 15, 2016, challenging CAE's tax treatment of the SADI disbursements. The scientific eligibility of Project Falcon's activities under subsection 248(1) of the ITA was not among the issues before the Tax Court; the dispute concerned exclusively the characterization of the SADI amounts. Rather, the Minister asserted that the amounts of $57,084,395 and $59,148,888 that CAE received or was entitled to receive under the SADI Agreement in its 2012 and 2013 taxation years, respectively, constituted "government assistance" pursuant to subsection 127(9).

This characterization triggered a severe, three-pronged statutory adjustment against CAE. First, the portions of the SADI contributions that CAE used to pay SR&ED expenditures—$41,003,491 in 2012 and $40,652,951 in 2013—were subtracted from CAE's deductible SR&ED expenditures pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(d) of the ITA. Second, CAE's SR&ED expenditures eligible for ITC purposes were reduced by the full amounts received or receivable under the SADI Agreement—$57,084,395 in 2012 and $59,148,888 in 2013—pursuant to subsection 127(18) of the ITA, resulting in a substantial clawback of SR&ED ITCs. Third, pursuant to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(iv) and 12(1)(x)(v) of the ITA, the Minister included $14,806,939 in CAE's income for the 2012 taxation year only, representing the difference between the amount CAE received in 2012 under the SADI Agreement ($55,810,430) and CAE's SR&ED expenditures in connection with the Agreement that year ($41,003,491).
Governing Statutory Framework in Canada

The Canadian SR&ED tax incentive regime is structured to subsidize net, at-risk private-sector expenditures on technological advancement, preventing double-dipping whereby a taxpayer claims federal tax credits on capital already provided by a public authority through a strict statutory mechanism integrating Sections 12, 37, and 127 of the ITA. The centrepiece of this mechanism is subsection 127(9), which defines "government assistance" expansively as "assistance from a government, municipality or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance or as any other form of assistance," excluding only deductions under subsection 127(5) or 127(6) (i.e., the investment tax credit itself).

Once an inflow is classified as government assistance under subsection 127(9), paragraph 37(1)(d) mandates that a taxpayer's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried forward or deducted in the year must be reduced by the total of all amounts of government assistance or non-government assistance that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Operating in tandem with paragraph 37(1)(d), subsection 127(18) reduces a taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" base for SR&ED ITC calculations by the amount of any government or non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date. Furthermore, paragraph 12(1)(x)—specifically subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv), read together with the limitations in subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)—functions as a statutory catch-all requiring a taxpayer to include in computing income from a business or property any particular amount received in the year from a government, municipality, or other public authority where the amount can reasonably be considered to have been received as a refund, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance, or as assistance—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, allowance, or any other form of assistance—in respect of an outlay or expense, to the extent that the particular amount was not otherwise included in income or deducted in computing a balance of undeducted outlays and does not reduce the cost of property or the amount of the outlay or expense. Only in the taxation year in which the taxpayer actually repays the government assistance under a legal obligation to do so can the repaid amount be added back to the SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) or deducted from income under paragraph 20(1)(hh), with the repaid amount also added to the investment tax credit under subsection 127(10.7).

cells: Tax Court of Canada (Trial)
CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57 (2021 CCI 57); Docket 2016-4984(IT)G
Justice Sylvain Ouimet (Decided Sept. 13/14, 2021)

Whether the SADI contributions received or receivable in 2012 and 2013 constituted "government assistance" under s. 127(9), including CAE's argument that the agreement was a simple loan under art. 2314 C.C.Q. and that loan proceeds are not "received" absent a transfer of ownership; whether the interest-rate differential alone could be government assistance was not before the Court, both parties having declined to address it.

Appeal Dismissed with Costs: Although characterized as a loan, the SADI Agreement was not an "ordinary business agreement" because its implicit ~2.5% rate of return was significantly below market; the amounts received in 2012 and 2013 were "government assistance" under s. 127(9) and the amounts receivable were government assistance for s. 127(18); the alternative s. 12(1)(x)(iii)/(iv) issue was not decided.
Federal Court of Appeal
CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (2022 CAF 178); Docket A-264-21
Boivin J.A., de Montigny J.A., Locke J.A. (Oct. 19, 2022)
Whether the TCC erred in refusing to bifurcate the SADI contribution into a non-taxable capital loan and a taxable interest-rate subsidy.
Appeal Dismissed from the Bench with Costs: No support in legislation or jurisprudence for bifurcating a non-commercial government loan.
Supreme Court of Canada
CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, SCC Docket 40504
Leave Panel of the Supreme Court of Canada (May 25, 2023)
Application for leave to appeal from the judgment of the Federal Court of Appeal in 2022 FCA 178.
Leave to Appeal Dismissed: Affirming the finality of the TCC and FCA rulings across Canada.

body.text: The Courts' Final Holding

Both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal ruled decisively in favour of the Crown, dismissing CAE's appeals with costs. Justice Ouimet of the TCC held (at paragraphs 116, 137, and 143) that, because the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) extends to "any other form of assistance," a repayable loan can constitute government assistance, and that the decisive question is whether the payments were made to promote the business interests of the payer pursuant to an "ordinary business agreement". Because the SADI Agreement's implicit rate of return of approximately 2.5%—below even the 3.65% risk-free Government of Canada bond rate as at March 30, 2009—was significantly lower than the market rate of return for a comparable loan, such that it would have been contrary to the business interests of a private lender to grant it, the amounts paid to CAE in 2012 and 2013 constituted "government assistance".

On appeal, CAE conceded that the SADI Agreement was in the nature of government assistance, but argued that the TCC erred in failing to distinguish between the repayable capital loan principal and the concessional interest-rate differential. Delivering judgment from the bench on October 19, 2022, Justice Boivin of the FCA rejected this bifurcation theory entirely, holding that Justice Ouimet properly applied settled appellate jurisprudence—namely Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co., [1987] 2 F.C. 60, Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., [1996] F.C.J. No. 1226 (QL) (1996 CanLII 11571), and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196—and that neither the ITA nor the case law permits carving out the principal of a non-commercial government loan from subsection 127(9).
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

Unlike routine SR&ED appeals where taxpayers fail at the threshold of subsection 248(1) due to an inability to prove technological uncertainty, a lack of systematic experimentation, or an absence of contemporaneous technical records, CAE's disqualification arose from a sophisticated statutory funding and contractual characterization failure. While Project Falcon was an SR&ED project bearing on the development of flight simulator and health sector technologies, CAE's legal, contractual, and evidentiary execution suffered from four fatal deficiencies that triggered the funded-research exclusions under subsection 127(9), paragraph 37(1)(d), subsection 127(18), and subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).
Failure 1: Misconstruing the Scope of "Any Other Form of Assistance" and Relying on Unconditional Repayability

CAE's primary legal argument at the trial level was that the SADI Agreement constituted a simple loan within the meaning of article 2314 of the Civil Code of Québec—$250,000,000 advanced over five years that CAE undertook to repay unconditionally—and that loan proceeds cannot have been "received" as "government assistance" because, under subsections 127(9) and 127(18), receipt requires a transfer of ownership, which does not occur under a loan. Relying on Dunkelman v. M.N.R. and Fonthill Lumber Ltd. v. The Queen, CAE posited that property is not transferred when a loan is made because the lender will eventually be repaid.

Justice Ouimet dismantled this argument: although he agreed that the SADI Agreement was a loan under article 2314 C.C.Q., he held, relying on the Le Robert and Merriam-Webster dictionary definitions, that "to receive" means simply to come into possession, so that no transfer of ownership is required, found Dunkelman inapplicable, and then assessed the agreement under the appellate test developed in Consumers' Gas, CCLC Technologies, and Immunovaccine. In Consumers' Gas, the Appeal Division of the Federal Court held that payments made by public authorities in exactly the same way and for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private businesses—that is, for the purpose of advancing the interests of the payor—do not constitute assistance, the word "assistance" carrying the colour of a grant or subsidy. Subsequently, in CCLC Technologies, the Federal Court of Appeal applied this test to find that an agreement serving public-policy objectives rather than the payer's business interests was not an ordinary business arrangement, and in Immunovaccine it confirmed that the words "or as any other form of assistance" give the word "assistance" a broad meaning capable of encompassing agreements that are not purely gratuitous and unilateral. By treating unconditional repayability as a legal shield against subsection 127(9) while ignoring the non-commercial nature of the SADI facility, CAE misjudged the governing legal test in Canada.
Failure 2: Contractual and Economic Deficiencies Proving the Absence of an "Ordinary Business Arrangement"

To escape classification as "government assistance" under the Consumers' Gas and CCLC Technologies test, a taxpayer must show that the payments were made pursuant to an "ordinary business agreement"—that a private business would have entered into the agreement to promote its business interests—which the Court assesses by comparing the agreement's terms with those of comparable agreements between private parties; notably, Justice Ouimet held that the government's public-policy motivation alone is not sufficient to establish that an agreement is not an ordinary business agreement. The evidentiary record before the TCC revealed multiple contractual features in SADI Agreement No. 780-503924 that were fundamentally incompatible with commercial debt. Testimony from Mr. Lemieux, Manager and Senior Investment Analyst at the Department of Industry Canada's Strategic Innovation Fund, who negotiated the SADI Agreement on behalf of the Minister of Industry, established that the SADI program was a federal "contribution" program designed to incentivize strategic aerospace and defence R&D in Canada, rather than a commercial lending operation seeking a market return on capital, the program having no target rate of return and requiring a reasonable return only to comply with World Trade Organization rules.

Moreover, as Justice Ouimet noted at paragraphs 20 and 79 of the Decision, the SADI Agreement imposed non-commercial restrictions on CAE. In exchange for contributions of up to $250,000,000 toward Project Falcon (equal to 35% of eligible expenses), CAE was contractually bound to manufacture all Project Falcon products exclusively in Canada, accept restrictions on transferring titles and intellectual property relating to the Project and on work performed and costs incurred outside Canada, notify the Minister of Industry of any other government assistance, establish a cooperation plan allocating at least 1.0% of the Project's eligible SR&ED expenditures to accredited Canadian post-secondary institutions, assume public-communications obligations, and submit periodic reports on SR&ED progress, results achieved, and program yields. Commercial banks and institutional debt funds do not impose sovereign industrial-policy covenants in arm's-length credit facilities. The financial architecture of the SADI Agreement also deviated sharply from commercial debt markets. Rather than charging a market interest rate commensurate with the risk of an unsecured instrument with an approximately 20-year term (a five-year contribution period followed by a 15-year repayment period, with no payments of interest or principal during the first five years), the SADI Agreement carried an implicit rate of return of approximately 2.5%—about 1.15% below the 3.65% risk-free Government of Canada bond rate as at March 30, 2009, and well below the 7.15% rate on CAE's own unsecured 2010 private placement. Furthermore, although CAE's initial October 2008 proposal contemplated a conditional reimbursement based on a 0.28% royalty rate applied to sales, CAE ultimately chose the unconditional option in the final agreement executed on March 30, 2009: repayment of 1.35 times the contributions received ($337,500,000 in total) in 15 fixed annual instalments due by July 31 of each year from 2015 to 2029, with no security. Requiring an unsecured, deferred repayment with an implicit yield below even the risk-free rate confirmed that the Crown was providing concessional financial aid rather than acting as a commercial creditor.
Failure 3: Evidentiary Backfire of Expert Valuation and the Unsubstantiated Bifurcation Theory

It was the respondent Crown—not CAE—that retained an expert witness, Neil de Gray, Director of Disputes and Investigations at Duff & Phelps, whom the Court recognized as an expert in corporate finance and the valuation of debt instruments; CAE produced no expert report or rebuttal report. Mr. de Gray's mandate was to determine whether the SADI Agreement constituted an "ordinary business agreement," and he concluded that its implicit rate of return of approximately 2.5% was significantly lower than the fair market rate for an instrument with a comparable risk profile, that it lacked the financial covenants typical of commercial agreements, and that it contained conditions motivated by political rather than business considerations.

Far from rescuing CAE's claim, CAE's own financial reporting created a devastating evidentiary paradox. As its Vice-President of Finance, Constantino Malatesta, testified, CAE had discounted the SADI contributions in its GAAP financial statements using fair market rates ranging from 6% to 13%, and recorded the $122,975,399 difference between the interest payable at market rates ($210,475,399) and the $87,500,000 actually payable under the Agreement as a "government benefit"—an acknowledgment, noted by Mr. de Gray and the Court, that the SADI Agreement was granted at a below-market rate. At trial, however, CAE did not advance the bifurcation argument: when invited by the Court, both CAE and the Crown declined to address whether the dollar value of the interest-rate differential alone could constitute "government assistance," treating that question as not before the Court; only before the Federal Court of Appeal did CAE argue that a distinction had to be made between the capital loan and the interest-rate differential. Justice Ouimet therefore did not rule on this proposition, and Justice Boivin, writing for a unanimous panel at the FCA, rejected it. As the FCA held at paragraph 4 of 2022 FCA 178, the TCC judge properly applied the authoritative case law and committed no palpable and overriding error in relying on the evidence, and the Court was unable to find support for CAE's proposed distinction in either the case law or the legislation. Neither the text of subsections 127(9), 37(1)(d), or 12(1)(x) nor Canadian appellate precedent provides any mechanism for unbundling a single hybrid government contribution into a non-taxable debt component and a taxable interest subsidy.
Failure 4: Project Governance and Accounting Integration Between SADI Cost Claims and SR&ED Tax Pools

A critical operational deficiency highlighted by the facts of CAE Inc. lies in how the taxpayer integrated its SADI contribution claims directly into its SR&ED tax credit pool for Project Falcon. Under the SADI Agreement, Industry Canada reimbursed a fixed percentage of eligible SR&ED costs incurred specifically in connection with Project Falcon. Mr. Lemieux's own audit for Industry Canada concerned CAE's funding proposal—verifying that the information it contained complied with departmental standards as part of a due-diligence and risk analysis—while, under the SADI Program, SR&ED projects were monitored annually or quarterly and an audit was performed whenever a claim for reimbursement of SR&ED expenditures was filed.

Because the SADI contributions were defined in the agreement as "financial assistance" intended to fund CAE's SR&ED activities on Project Falcon, the amounts received or receivable ($57,084,395 in 2012 and $59,148,888 in 2013) reduced qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18), and the portions actually used to pay SR&ED expenditures ($41,003,491 and $40,652,951) reduced deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d). This direct linkage caused a significant double impact: the SADI amounts reduced CAE's SR&ED expenditure pool and ITC base in 2012 and 2013, while the $14,806,939 of 2012 receipts not applied to SR&ED expenditures was included in income under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv), leaving CAE to recover deductions and credits only as it makes its fixed annual repayments, scheduled from 2015 to 2029.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement adjudicated in CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 178) against CAE's specific legal, contractual, and evidentiary failures and the authoritative standard of proof enforced by the Canadian courts.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Determination

cells: Exemption from "Government Assistance" as an Ordinary Business Arrangement
ITA s. 127(9); Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co., [1987] 2 F.C. 60; Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., [1996] F.C.J. No. 1226 (QL); Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196.

CAE argued that the $250M SADI facility for Project Falcon was a simple loan under art. 2314 C.C.Q. Failed because SADI Agreement No. 780-503924 carried an implicit return of approximately 2.5% (below the 3.65% risk-free rate), was unsecured with a five-year repayment deferral, and imposed non-commercial Canadian manufacturing, IP-transfer, and post-secondary collaboration covenants.

Ordinary Business Agreement Standard: The taxpayer must show that a private business would have entered into the agreement to promote its business interests; the Court compares the agreement's terms with comparable private agreements, and the government's public-policy motive alone is not decisive. For CAE, the ~2.5% implicit return, significantly below market, was determinative.
Scope of "Any Other Form of Assistance" Respecting Non-Forgivable Loans
ITA s. 127(9) ("whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan... or as any other form of assistance").
CAE relied on the loan characterization under art. 2314 C.C.Q. and argued that loan proceeds are not "received" as government assistance because a loan involves no transfer of ownership.

Substance of Concessional Terms Over Repayability: A government loan need not be forgivable or conditional to be "government assistance." Any repayable loan with non-commercial terms falls within "any other form of assistance".
Valuation & Bifurcation of Hybrid Concessional Financing (Principal vs. Interest Subsidy)
ITA s. 127(9), s. 37(1)(d), s. 12(1)(x); Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33 (standard of appellate review).

The Crown's expert (Neil de Gray, Duff & Phelps) showed the ~2.5% implicit return was well below market, and CAE's own financial statements recorded a $122,975,399 "government benefit"; at trial both parties declined to address whether only the interest differential was assistance, and on appeal CAE argued that only the interest subsidy—not the loan principal—was "government assistance".

All-or-Nothing Characterization Standard: The FCA found no support in the ITA or Canadian case law for distinguishing the capital loan from the interest-rate differential. Once found non-commercial, the amounts received are government assistance.
Reduction of Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool & Qualified Expenditures for ITCs
ITA s. 37(1)(d), s. 127(9), and s. 127(18).
CAE claimed SR&ED deductions and ITCs on Project Falcon expenditures in 2012 and 2013 without reducing them by the SADI contributions, which it treated as loan proceeds.

Direct Nexus ("In Respect Of" SR&ED) Standard: Where government assistance is contractually tied to funding SR&ED project costs, the amounts received or receivable reduce s. 127(18) qualified expenditures ($57,084,395 and $59,148,888), and the portions used for SR&ED expenditures reduce the s. 37(1)(d) pool ($41,003,491 and $40,652,951) in the year received/receivable.
Income Inclusion of Unapplied Government Assistance Upon Receipt
ITA s. 12(1)(x)(iv), read with s. 12(1)(x)(v) (and s. 20(1)(hh) / s. 37(1)(c) upon subsequent repayment).
CAE treated SADI disbursements as balance-sheet debt liabilities rather than taxable income receipts in 2012 and 2013.

Statutory Receipt Inclusion Standard: Any government assistance received in respect of an outlay or expense that does not otherwise reduce the cost of property or deductible SR&ED pools must be included in taxable income in the year of receipt under s. 12(1)(x)(iv); for CAE, $14,806,939 was included for 2012.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

Before examining the applied case studies, senior Canadian tax advisors must contextualize CAE Inc. within the subsequent legislative evolution of the ITA. Because the Supreme Court of Canada refused leave to appeal in May 2023, the CAE Inc. doctrine threatened to claw back SR&ED and clean economy ITCs across Canada whenever corporations accessed federal or provincial low-interest loan programs. In response, the Department of Finance announced legislative amendments in the 2023 Fall Economic Statement, released on November 21, 2023, to amend subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x), providing that a bona fide concessional loan carrying low or zero interest from a public authority will generally be excluded from "government assistance" if it is repayable on reasonable repayment terms. These amendments were enacted by the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1 (Bill C-69), which received royal assent on June 20, 2024: the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) now excludes an "excluded loan" as defined in subsection 12(11)—a loan, other than a forgivable loan, evidenced in writing, from a government, municipality or other public authority in Canada, for which bona fide arrangements were made at the time the loan was made for repayment within a reasonable time, and the funds from which were used to earn income from a business or property—and new subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix), which excludes amounts received as an excluded loan from income inclusion, applies to loans made after December 31, 2019.

Despite this statutory relief for conventional fixed-schedule debt, the judicial trap established in CAE Inc. remains lethal for Canadian taxpayers in two pervasive scenarios. First, the trap applies wherever a government funding agreement is structured as a royalty-contingent contribution, revenue-sharing facility, or hybrid instrument that lacks fixed, unconditional debt-repayment schedules and therefore fails the statutory requirement for "reasonable repayment terms" of a bona fide loan. Second, the trap applies wherever a taxpayer enters into multi-party public procurement or state-backed development contracts without segregating commercial deliverables and general financing from SR&ED cost-reimbursement pools. The following two remedial case studies illustrate how Canadian enterprises facing the exact pitfalls identified in CAE Inc. can restructure their project governance, contract terms, technical documentation, and experimentation tracking to achieve comprehensive SR&ED compliance.
Case Study 1: Aerospace & Defence Autonomous Avionics Developer (Restructuring Hybrid SADI/SIP Contributions and Isolating SR&ED Work Packages)
Industry Scenario and Initial CAE Inc. Pitfalls

AeroVanguard Systems Inc. (AeroVanguard), a Canadian-controlled corporation based in Montreal, Quebec, is developing a next-generation autonomous fly-by-wire actuator and real-time sensor-fusion flight simulator ("Project Horizon") over a four-year period with a total budget of $80,000,000. To finance Project Horizon, AeroVanguard negotiates a $30,000,000 funding package with a federal innovation agency modelled on the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) framework. In its initial draft agreement, the federal agency proposes a single "Repayable Contribution Agreement" that mirrors, and in some respects goes beyond, the features found to be non-commercial in CAE Inc. Under the draft terms, the agency reimburses 37.5% of AeroVanguard's eligible SR&ED costs on Project Horizon, while repayment is calculated as a 2.5% royalty on AeroVanguard's gross commercial sales over a 15-year post-project period, yielding an effective interest rate of 3.2%. The draft agreement also imposes strict Canadian industrial-benefit covenants and subjects all Project Horizon engineering logs and payroll records to federal contribution audits. Concurrently, AeroVanguard's engineering team tracks Project Horizon in a single Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) cost centre, co-mingling routine systems-integration engineering, commercial prototype fabrication, and core algorithmic SR&ED.

Under CAE Inc. (2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 178) and even under the post-2023 bona fide loan rules, this draft structure is a severe tax liability. Because repayment is contingent on gross sales royalties rather than fixed debt amortization, the arrangement fails to qualify as a bona fide loan with reasonable debt repayment terms, and its 3.2% effective rate and industrial-policy covenants fail the Consumers' Gas and CCLC Technologies test for an "ordinary business arrangement". Consequently, the entire $30,000,000 disbursement will be deemed "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), wiping out $30,000,000 of AeroVanguard's paragraph 37(1)(d) SR&ED pool and subsection 127(18) ITC base, while triggering immediate income inclusion under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) for any excess.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Contractual Unbundling and Debt Restructuring (Overcoming the Anti-Bifurcation Rule)

In CAE Inc., the Federal Court of Appeal held that a court cannot ex post facto bifurcate a single hybrid contribution agreement into a loan component and a subsidy component. Therefore, AeroVanguard must execute ex ante contractual separation prior to signing by splitting the $30,000,000 financing into two distinct legal instruments. Rather than accepting a royalty-linked contribution covering the entire $30,000,000, AeroVanguard negotiates a standalone $24,000,000 Senior Term Loan Agreement ("Instrument A"), executed either through a commercial syndicate co-lending with Export Development Canada or the Business Development Bank of Canada at a benchmark commercial floating rate, or as an unconditional fixed-schedule term loan satisfying the statutory bona fide loan criteria. Crucially, Instrument A eliminates all sales-royalty contingencies, mandates fixed principal and interest amortization dates independent of Project Horizon's commercial success, and states explicitly that loan proceeds are provided for general corporate working capital and capital expenditures rather than as a reimbursement of specific SR&ED expenses.

Simultaneously, the remaining $6,000,000 of concessional public-policy support is isolated into a separate contribution agreement ("Instrument B") restricted exclusively to non-SR&ED commercialization activities, facility expansion, and manufacturing tooling, which are already ineligible for SR&ED ITCs under the ITA. By contractually prohibiting Instrument B funds from being claimed against SR&ED wages or subcontractor costs, AeroVanguard prevents the $6,000,000 assistance from contaminating the paragraph 37(1)(d) SR&ED pool.
Step 2: Project Governance and ERP Cost-Centre Segregation

To prevent the kind of overlap seen in CAE Inc., where SADI contributions defined as financial assistance for Project Falcon's SR&ED activities, and verified through Industry Canada's claim-by-claim audits, flowed directly against the same SR&ED expenditures, AeroVanguard's tax and finance leadership restructures the ERP chart of accounts into hermetically sealed work breakdown structures (WBS). The primary account, WBS-100 (Core SR&ED — Self-Funded), is dedicated strictly to resolving technological uncertainties eligible under subsection 248(1), such as non-linear aerodynamic control-law instability during supersonic-to-subsonic transition, and is funded 100% out of AeroVanguard's general corporate treasury and Instrument A debt proceeds. A secondary account, WBS-200 (Non-SR&ED Commercial Engineering & Tooling — Government Assisted), is dedicated to routine CAD design, commercial flight-deck human-factors certification, and production tooling, with all eligible cost submissions under Instrument B ($6,000,000) mapped exclusively to WBS-200 invoices and payroll. To reinforce this accounting separation, the corporate Board of Directors adopts a formal SR&ED Cost Allocation Resolution prior to the start of the fiscal year prohibiting the cross-charging of WBS-200 subsidized personnel hours or material invoices to WBS-100.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Technological Uncertainty (Subsection 248(1) Compliance)

To ensure that WBS-100 withstands CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) scrutiny on the scientific merits, AeroVanguard implements a contemporaneous technical documentation protocol structured around the foundational criteria of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence. At the inception of each fiscal quarter, the Lead Avionics Architect authors a Technical Baseline & Uncertainty Dossier documenting why publicly available aerodynamic control models and commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) Kalman filter algorithms fail to resolve a specific system-level constraint—namely, achieving sub-4-millisecond latency in multi-sensor fusion under extreme electromagnetic interference (EMI) without inducing actuator oscillation. Concurrently, all standard DO-178C software verification and routine hardware debugging are explicitly logged as non-SR&ED and routed to WBS-200.
Step 4: Systematic Experimentation Tracking and Contemporaneous Evidence

AeroVanguard configures its Jira and Git version-control repositories to generate contemporaneous, date-stamped evidence linking every hour of WBS-100 labour to a structured process of experimentation. Every experimental iteration is logged as a formal Hypothesis-Test-Analysis Ticket (HTAT) containing a quantified scientific hypothesis (for example, postulating that implementing an adaptive unscented Kalman filter with dynamic covariance pruning will reduce state-estimation latency from 9.2 ms to under 3.8 ms under 40 V/m EMI), the exact simulation or wind-tunnel test protocol executed, raw telemetry data and failure logs, and the analytical conclusion formulating the next hypothesis. Bi-weekly timesheets require engineers to allocate hours directly to specific HTAT numbers within WBS-100, signed off contemporaneously by the Vice President of Engineering, providing an unassailable audit trail proving both scientific eligibility under subsection 248(1) and complete financial insulation from subsection 127(9) government assistance.
Case Study 2: Clean-Tech Solid-State Battery & Grid Storage Manufacturer (Remediating Multi-Party Public Procurement and Concessional Green Financing)
Industry Scenario and Initial CAE Inc. Pitfalls

VoltCore Energy Corp. (VoltCore), an advanced battery-materials and grid-storage manufacturer in Mississauga, Ontario, is executing a three-year R&D program ("Project Cathode-X") to develop a lithium-metal solid-state electrolyte capable of operating at −40°C for northern Canadian microgrids. VoltCore enters into a bipartite arrangement with a provincial Crown utility agency and a federal clean-technology agency providing $15,000,000 in financing. Under the initial draft agreement, the agencies advance $15,000,000 as an "Unconditionally Repayable Green Innovation Advance" carrying a 0% interest rate during the three-year R&D phase and a 1.5% interest rate thereafter, with principal repayments deferred until VoltCore achieves a cumulative EBITDA threshold of $20,000,000. In addition, the agreement grants the provincial Crown utility agency a right of first refusal to purchase the first 50 megawatt-hours (MWh) of commercial battery units at a 20% discount to market price, and requires VoltCore to submit quarterly SR&ED progress reports to the agencies to trigger each $2,500,000 funding tranche.

VoltCore initially plans to claim full federal SR&ED ITCs and provincial Ontario R&D tax credits on the $15,000,000 spent on Project Cathode-X, arguing that the advance is a repayable loan and alternatively that at worst, only the below-market interest subsidy should reduce its SR&ED pool. Under CAE Inc., VoltCore's position will be summarily defeated on two grounds. First, VoltCore's fallback argument that only the interest-rate differential between 0%/1.5% and its commercial borrowing rate constitutes assistance is barred by the FCA's anti-bifurcation holding in 2022 FCA 178. Second, because principal repayment is contingent upon achieving a $20,000,000 EBITDA threshold and is coupled with a non-commercial 20% product discount and SR&ED milestone disbursements, the arrangement is neither an "ordinary business arrangement" under Consumers' Gas and CCLC Technologies nor a bona fide unconditional loan with fixed reasonable repayment terms. The CRA will classify the entire $15,000,000 as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9)—or as a "contract payment" where the Crown agency acquires commercial rights—eliminating VoltCore's SR&ED pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) and assessing immediate tax under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring into an Ordinary Commercial Supply Contract and a Bona Fide Loan

To satisfy both the Consumers' Gas commerciality standard and the statutory bona fide loan regime, VoltCore's tax counsel splits and rewrites the contractual architecture before any funds are advanced. For the $12,000,000 federal clean-tech agency debt facility, VoltCore removes the $20,000,000 EBITDA repayment condition entirely, replacing it with an unconditional Promissory Note and Term Loan Agreement featuring a fixed maturity date seven years from drawdown and a mandatory, non-contingent amortization schedule commencing in Year 4, backed by corporate covenants customary in commercial debt markets. Furthermore, funding drawdowns are decoupled from SR&ED expenditure reimbursements and tied instead to balance-sheet liquidity ratios.

For the $3,000,000 provided by the provincial Crown utility agency, VoltCore restructures the arrangement as an arm's-length Commercial Supply Agreement for future commercial battery packs priced at full fair market value, eliminating the 20% below-market discount. The contract explicitly specifies that VoltCore retains 100% of all foreground and background intellectual property (IP) generated during Project Cathode-X, that the Crown utility is purchasing standardized commercial battery hardware post-development rather than commissioning or funding SR&ED on its behalf—thereby preventing the receipt from being classified as a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9)—and that the pricing reflects ordinary commercial terms verified by independent valuation benchmarks.
Step 2: Project Governance and Tranche Timing Optimization (Subsection 127(18) & Repayment Synchronization)

In the event any residual municipal or provincial grant cannot be avoided, VoltCore's tax governance committee actively manages the statutory timing rules of paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18). Under subsection 127(18), government assistance reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures if it is received, entitled to be received, or can reasonably be expected to be received on or before the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year, which falls six months after fiscal year-end. VoltCore structures any non-repayable grant agreements so that eligibility is strictly restricted to specific, ring-fenced sub-projects—such as environmental lifecycle assessment and pilot-line safety certification—that are excluded from the Form T661 SR&ED claim, ensuring zero overlap between the grant's eligible expenditure schedule and VoltCore's SR&ED cost pool. Furthermore, where VoltCore holds any legacy repayable government assistance from prior years caught by the CAE Inc. rule, VoltCore's tax team schedules contractual repayments prior to fiscal year-end to immediately trigger the statutory add-back to the SR&ED pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and the corresponding addition to its investment tax credit under subsection 127(10.7).
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Material-Science Technological Uncertainty

To substantiate the scientific eligibility of Project Cathode-X under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, VoltCore mandates a rigorous Electrochemical SR&ED Protocol. Prior to synthesizing new solid-state electrolyte formulations, the Chief Battery Scientist documents the precise scientific knowledge gap, explaining why existing sulfide- and oxide-based solid electrolytes exhibit severe lithium-dendrite propagation and interfacial impedance spikes exceeding 500 Ω·cm² when cycled below −20°C at current densities exceeding 0.5 mA/cm². The documentation clearly separates scientific advancement—specifically, formulating a novel halide-doped argyrodite crystal lattice to stabilize ionic conductivity at −40°C—from commercial product development, such as designing the outer thermal-enclosure casing for the utility microgrid.
Step 4: Structured Experimentation Tracking and Material Disposition Auditing

Because chemical and material-science SR&ED claims frequently face CRA challenges regarding materials consumed versus materials transformed under subsection 127(9), VoltCore implements an automated Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) and Material Ledger. Each experimental electrolyte synthesis batch is assigned a unique LIMS identifier recording the exact stoichiometric hypothesis, sintering temperature profile, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging of dendrite formation, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test results. Every gram of lithium precursor and solid electrolyte consumed and rendered unusable during destructive low-temperature cycling tests is logged contemporaneously in a scrap-disposition ledger with photographic and weight-ticket verification, whereas any pilot cells delivered under the Commercial Supply Agreement to the provincial utility are tracked in commercial inventory accounts and excluded from the SR&ED claim.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian Tax Advisors

The Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal decisions in CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 178) closed the door on two taxpayer strategies in Canada: the TCC rejected the argument that characterizing non-commercial government funding as an unconditionally repayable loan—and therefore as not "received" for lack of a transfer of ownership—insulates it from subsection 127(9), and the FCA rejected the attempt to bifurcate hybrid government financing into a non-taxable capital loan and a taxable interest-rate differential. When a financing agreement executed with a public authority fails the strict commerciality standard of Consumers' Gas, CCLC Technologies, and Immunovaccine—or fails to qualify as a bona fide unconditional loan with fixed, reasonable debt-repayment terms under post-2023 statutory rules—the consequences are draconian: the assistance relating to SR&ED expenditures reduces the taxpayer's deductible SR&ED pool under paragraph 37(1)(d), the amounts received or receivable reduce qualified expenditures, and therefore SR&ED ITCs, under subsection 127(18), and any amount received but not applied against SR&ED expenditures is included in income under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).

For Canadian R&D tax counsel and corporate tax directors, the imperative is clear. Tax advisory intervention cannot wait until T661 claim preparation or CRA audit defence; it must occur at the contract-drafting stage of government funding negotiations. By eliminating sales-royalty and EBITDA repayment contingencies, unbundling general corporate debt facilities from targeted non-SR&ED grants, enforcing strict ERP cost-centre firewalls between assisted and unassisted work packages, and maintaining contemporaneous hypothesis-driven experimentation records, Canadian innovators can secure public-sector capital while fully preserving their statutory entitlement to SR&ED tax incentives.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; TCC held non-commercial repayable loans were government assistance reducing ITCs and included in income.
